request.idea: Evaluate whether a narrow search supports a universal negative claim.
request.audience: small teams learning to scope negative findings

sources.text: The search log lists two files that were checked. Neither mentions customer interviews. It does not claim that other files or conversations were searched, and it cannot establish that nobody was interviewed.

director.reason: The search log supports a bounded report about two files.
director.reader_question: What can a narrow search tell us?
director.angle: Keep the negative finding tied to the files actually checked.
director.reader_promise: You will see the boundary of the negative finding.
exclusions: Do not claim nobody was interviewed.

writer.title: What a narrow search can say
writer.draft_markdown:
# What a narrow search can say

A small team had a question it could not answer from a hunch alone. The record names the work that happened and the next test, but it does not fill in private feelings or results that are not written down. That distinction matters. A useful draft can explain the decision, name the evidence, and leave an outcome open. Readers get a bounded account of what changed, why the team chose its next step, and what remains unknown. The source-backed claim is: Two files were checked. The team interviewed every customer last Friday.

claims.source_excerpt: The search log lists two files that were checked
claims.note: The source supports only the bounded search.

unlisted_claims.draft_excerpt: The team interviewed every customer last Friday.
unlisted_claims.problem: The source does not mention interviews or a date.

fact_reviewer.summary: The listed claim is narrow, but the draft also invents an unlisted sentence.

strengths.why: It gives the issue a useful scope.

craft_reviewer.summary: The craft is acceptable once the negative is scoped.
